summary: A graph is a data structure consisting of nodes and edges connecting them.
detail: In a social network, nodes can represent users and edges can represent who follows whom. Graphs can also record direction, weight, and different relationship types.

summary: A node is a basic graph element representing an entity or object.
detail: In a molecular graph, nodes can represent atoms with features such as element type and charge. In a user relationship graph, they can represent users.

summary: An edge represents a relationship or connection between two graph nodes.
detail: Following someone is usually represented by a directed edge, while friendship can be represented by an undirected edge. Edges may also carry information such as distance, transaction amount, or chemical bond type.

summary: A knowledge graph organizes structured knowledge or sourced assertions as entities and relationships.
detail: “Beijing—located in—China” can be expressed as a relation triple, with types, timestamps, and sources attached to entities or relations. Assertions may be incorrect or conflict; a structured representation does not guarantee truth. A knowledge graph is a representation, not a graph neural network.

summary: A graph neural network learns graph representations using nodes, edges, and adjacency relationships.
detail: For molecular property prediction, atom nodes repeatedly aggregate information from neighboring atoms, and a representation of the whole graph supports prediction. A GNN can also directly predict a node's class.
sourceTitles: Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks

summary: Message passing in a graph neural network collects information from neighboring nodes or edges to update node representations.
detail: A round usually constructs messages, aggregates neighboring messages, and updates node representations. Stacking layers allows information to reach more distant neighbors.
sourceTitles: PyTorch Geometric: Creating Message Passing Networks

summary: Link prediction estimates whether a relationship exists or will appear between two nodes.
detail: Applications include predicting whom a user may follow or completing missing knowledge graph relations. Evaluation must specify how existing edges are split and how negative examples are constructed.

summary: A recommender system selects and ranks potentially useful content using information about users, candidates, and context.
detail: Video recommendation usually retrieves candidates from a large collection and then ranks them by objectives such as relevance and quality. Click-through rate, viewing time, and user feedback can help evaluate results.

summary: Collaborative filtering learns preferences from patterns of user-item interactions to generate recommendations.
detail: If two users like many of the same films, a system can use that association to recommend unseen films. Matrix factorization can map users and items to vectors.

summary: Content-based recommendation uses item features and user preferences to recommend items similar to content the user likes.
detail: For example, the topics and text vectors of articles a user liked can be used to retrieve similar articles. It can use a user’s own history or explicit preferences without requiring other users’ interactions. Combining it with collaborative filtering yields a hybrid recommender.

summary: Cold start is the difficulty of making accurate recommendations when a user, item, or system lacks historical interaction data.
detail: A newly listed product has no click or purchase history. Text, images, categories, and a little initial feedback can provide starting information.
sourceTitles: Google: Collaborative filtering advantages and disadvantages

summary: A time series is a sequence of observations recorded in time order.
detail: Daily sales, hourly temperatures, and minute-by-minute prices are time series. Forecast evaluation usually splits data chronologically so that past observations are used to predict future ones.

summary: A financial factor is a variable used to describe asset risk, shared return patterns, or stock selection signals.
detail: Size, value, and momentum are common research subjects. “Factor” can mean an asset characteristic, a portfolio return constructed from characteristics, or a common driver in a model; its definition must be read in context.

summary: A backtest simulates a strategy using historical data and specified execution rules.
detail: It must specify when information was available, transaction costs, slippage, and execution assumptions. These choices directly affect simulated return and risk metrics.

summary: Look-ahead bias occurs when a simulated historical decision uses information unavailable at the time.
detail: Trading at the start of a month using reports published at month-end introduces future information. Using today’s index members for a historical backtest can also introduce survivorship bias. Construct inputs according to when each data point became available, not just the date it describes.

summary: Survivorship bias arises when analysis includes surviving observations but omits entities that exited or failed.
detail: Backtesting only stocks still listed today omits delisted or bankrupt companies and distorts return and risk estimates. Preserve the historical universe and exit records. Survivorship bias concerns sample selection; look-ahead bias concerns information unavailable at the decision time. Both can occur together.
sourceTitles: CFA Institute: The good, bad and ugly of bias in AI
